title: Author, Audience, Purpose
bigQuestion: What makes a text sacred to a community, and what questions should a careful reader ask before deciding what it means?

story.title: Three Books Behind the Glass
story.kicker: A class on a field trip stops at one museum case and finds three sacred texts, each treated in a different way.
paragraphs: The field trip has reached the last gallery of the afternoon, and most of the class is tired. Then Ms. Ortiz stops them in front of a long glass case with soft lights. Inside are three objects. On the left, a scroll of pale parchment is rolled around two wooden handles, open just enough to show neat columns of Hebrew letters. In the middle, a book lies open on a carved wooden stand. Its pages are covered in flowing Arabic script, edged with gold and blue. On the right sits a stack of long, narrow strips of dried palm leaf, tied together with a cord through two holes.

Jordan leans close to the palm leaves. The writing is tiny and even, scratched into the leaf and darkened with ink. The card says it is a Buddhist text copied in South Asia a few hundred years ago. Each leaf is about the size of a ruler. Jordan counts the holes and wonders how anyone kept the pages in order. Ms. Ortiz points out that the cord through the holes is the answer. Untie it, and the book falls apart into loose leaves.

Amira stands at the middle stand. She recognizes the Arabic before she reads the card. At home, her family's copy of the Qur'an is kept on a high shelf, wrapped in cloth, and her grandmother washes before she opens it. She tells the class that the book in the case is beautiful, but it is strange to see it behind glass, where no one can recite from it. A museum guard nods. He says visitors from many faiths often say the same thing about objects in this room.

Ben looks at the scroll. His cousin read from a Torah scroll at her bat mitzvah last spring. He remembers that no one touched the letters with their fingers. The reader followed the words with a small silver pointer shaped like a hand. The scroll in the case is old and worn, and the card says that when a scroll becomes too damaged to use, many communities bury it with care instead of throwing it away.

Ms. Ortiz asks the class what the three objects have in common. They are made of different materials. They are written in different languages. They come from different traditions. But each one was copied by hand with great effort, and each one was treated by a community as something more than an ordinary book. The question for this unit, she says, is what makes a text sacred, and how an outsider can read one with care.
story.think: Amira says it feels strange to see the Qur'an behind glass. What does her reaction tell you about the difference between a museum object and a text a community uses?

lessons.title: A Text a Community Treasures
lessons.mainIdea: A text becomes sacred through the way a community receives it, treats it and lives by it, not only through what is written in it.
reading: In a Sikh gurdwara, or house of worship, the Guru Granth Sahib rests on a raised platform under a canopy, covered with embroidered cloth. In many gurdwaras, at night it is carried to a separate room to rest, and in the morning it is brought back with prayers. Sikhs treat the book this way because they regard it as their living Guru, or teacher. For Sikhs, the words are not only about the Guru. They are the Guru's presence among them.

Scholars of religion use the term *sacred text* for writing that a community sets apart as holy, authoritative or revealed. Another common term is *scripture*, from a Latin word for writings. A sacred text is not defined by its age or its beauty alone. Many old, beautiful books are not sacred to anyone. What makes a text sacred is a relationship: a community reads it, recites it, argues over it and shapes its life by it.

You can often see that relationship in how people handle the object. Many Jews read a Torah scroll with a pointer so that hands do not touch the letters. Many Muslims perform ritual washing before touching a printed Qur'an in Arabic and keep it off the floor. Christians in many churches carry the Gospel book in procession and stand for its reading. These acts of *reverence*, or deep respect, show outsiders what the text means to insiders.

This course studies sacred texts from the outside, as a scholar would. That means you will describe how each community treats its texts, and you will attribute each belief to the people who hold it. You do not have to share a belief to understand why it matters to someone else.

words.d: writing that a community sets apart as holy, authoritative or revealed
the sacred writings of a religious tradition; from a Latin word meaning writings
deep respect shown through words, actions or the careful handling of an object
a Sikh house of worship, where the Guru Granth Sahib is kept and read

look.title: Three Ways of Handling a Text
look.text: In a synagogue, a reader follows the Torah scroll with a silver pointer instead of a finger. In many Muslim homes, a copy of the Qur'an is kept on a high shelf and is not placed on the floor. In many gurdwaras, the Guru Granth Sahib rests under a canopy by day and is carried to its own room each night.
look.prompt: Pick one of these practices. What does it suggest about how that community understands its text?

check.q: According to the lesson, what mainly makes a text sacred?
choices: A community sets it apart and shapes its life by it
It is older than a thousand years
It is written in a language no one speaks today
It is kept in a museum
check.why: Scholars describe a sacred text by its relationship to a community that treats it as holy or authoritative, not by age or beauty alone.

check.q: Why do Sikhs treat the Guru Granth Sahib with the honor given to a person?
choices: They regard it as a history book about India
They regard it as their living Guru
They believe it was written by Moses
They use it only on holidays
check.why: Sikhs regard the Guru Granth Sahib as their living Guru, or teacher, so it rests under a canopy and is carried to rest each night.

check.q: A reader in a synagogue uses a pointer instead of a finger to follow the Torah scroll. This is an example of what?
check.why: Handling the scroll with a pointer so hands do not touch the letters is an act of reverence, or deep respect.

lessons.title: What Sacred Texts Do
lessons.mainIdea: Communities use sacred texts in worship, as guides for law and ethics, and as the story of who they are.
reading: Five times a day, Muslims around the world perform salat, the ritual prayer. In every prayer they recite the opening chapter of the Qur'an, the Fatiha, in Arabic. A Muslim in Chicago and a Muslim in Jakarta say the same words in the same language. Here the text works as *liturgy*, the set words of public worship. It is spoken and heard, not only read silently.

Sacred texts also guide action. Jewish law, or halakha, draws on the commandments of the Torah as the rabbis interpreted them. Muslim scholars draw on the Qur'an and the example of the Prophet to describe right conduct. Many Christians turn to the Sermon on the Mount when they think about forgiveness. In each case the text is an *authority*, a source that people consult when they ask how to live.

Finally, sacred texts tell communities who they are. At the Passover Seder, Jewish families retell the Exodus as their own story. Christians read the Gospels as the story of the person at the center of their faith. Hindus hear the Ramayana told in plays and festivals. A text like this gives a people its *identity*, a shared memory that joins the living to the past.

Most sacred texts do all three jobs at once. A single psalm can be sung in worship, quoted in an argument about justice and remembered as part of a people's history. When you meet a new text in this course, ask which of these jobs it does for the people who hold it sacred.

words.d: the set words and actions of public worship
a source people consult and trust when deciding what is right or true
a group's shared sense of who it is, often built from a common story and memory

look.title: How Many People Hold These Texts Sacred
look.cite: Rounded common estimates of adherents worldwide, early 2020s; figures vary by source
look.prompt: The Jewish and Sikh communities are small compared with the others. Why might a small community's text still matter a great deal to world history?

check.q: When Muslims recite the Fatiha in Arabic during every salat, the Qur'an is working mainly as what?
choices: Liturgy, the set words of worship
check.why: Reciting the Fatiha in each ritual prayer uses the Qur'an as liturgy, the set words of public worship.

check.q: Which example shows a sacred text acting as an authority for how to live?
choices: Rabbis drawing on Torah commandments to describe Jewish law
check.why: Halakha, Jewish law, draws on the Torah's commandments as the rabbis interpreted them, so the text serves as an authority.

check.q: At the Passover Seder, Jewish families retell the Exodus as their own story. Which job of a sacred text does this show most clearly?
choices: Identity, a shared memory of who a people is
check.why: Retelling the Exodus as a family's own story builds identity, a shared memory that joins the living to the past.

lessons.title: Who Wrote It?
lessons.mainIdea: Traditions often hold beliefs about who gave or wrote their texts, and scholars also study how texts were composed; a careful reader keeps both in view.
reading: Open a Qur'an and you will not find an author's name on the cover. Muslims believe the Qur'an is the word of God, revealed to the Prophet Muhammad through the angel Gabriel over about twenty-three years, from about 610 to 632 CE. In this view Muhammad is not the author but the one who received and recited it. The Arabic word qur'an itself means recitation. This belief about origin is called *revelation*, a message believed to come from God.

Other traditions describe origins in other ways. Jewish and Christian tradition long held that Moses wrote the Torah. Many modern scholars instead see it as the work of several writers and editors over centuries, combined into one text. Hindus describe the Vedas as shruti, meaning what was heard. In this view, ancient sages heard eternal truths and did not invent them. Many texts are *anonymous*, with no author named at all.

Some texts do name their writers. Scholars across many backgrounds agree that Paul wrote at least seven of the New Testament letters that bear his name, including Romans and Galatians. The Analects of Confucius were gathered by his students and their followers after his death. So *authorship* can mean one writer, a group of disciples, a long chain of editors or, for believers, a divine source.

In this course you will state both kinds of claims clearly and keep them apart. You might write, Muslims believe the Qur'an was revealed to Muhammad. You might write, many historians date this book to the sixth century BCE. Each sentence says who holds the view. Neither one asks you to decide which is true.

words.d: a message that believers hold was made known by God or a divine source
written by someone whose name is not given or not known
the question of who wrote, gave or shaped a text
in Hinduism, what was heard: the Vedas, understood as truths heard by ancient sages

look.title: Two Kinds of Sentences
look.text: Sentence A: Muslims believe the Qur'an was revealed to Muhammad over about twenty-three years. Sentence B: Many modern scholars think the Torah combines several earlier sources. Sentence C: The Qur'an was revealed to Muhammad. Sentence D: The Torah is a patchwork of sources.
look.prompt: Which two sentences fit an academic course, and what is missing from the other two?

check.q: How do Muslims understand Muhammad's role in relation to the Qur'an?
choices: He received and recited God's revelation
check.why: Muslims believe the Qur'an is God's word revealed to Muhammad through the angel Gabriel; he received and recited it.

check.q: What does the Hindu term shruti mean when applied to the Vedas?
choices: What was heard by ancient sages
check.why: Shruti means what was heard; Hindus describe the Vedas as eternal truths heard by ancient sages.

check.q: Which sentence is written the way this course asks you to write?
choices: Many modern scholars think the Torah combines several earlier sources.
The Torah is obviously a patchwork.
Moses certainly wrote every word of the Torah.
Nobody knows anything about the Torah.
check.why: The first sentence attributes the view to the people who hold it, which is how the academic study of religion states claims.

lessons.title: For Whom, When and Why?
lessons.mainIdea: Every text was first addressed to an audience at a certain time for a purpose, and knowing these helps a reader understand what it says.
reading: The Gospel of Luke begins in an unusual way. Before telling any story, the writer explains himself. He says many others have written accounts, and he has decided to write an orderly one for a reader named Theophilus. He even says why: so that Theophilus may know the certainty of what he has been taught. In four verses the author names his *audience* and his *purpose*.

Most texts are not so direct, but the same questions apply. The *audience* is the first group of readers or hearers. Paul's letter to the Galatians was sent to specific churches in a region of what is now Turkey. The Qur'an often addresses the Prophet or the early Muslim community directly, and many verses respond to events in Mecca or Medina. Knowing the first audience explains why a text mentions certain people, places or problems.

The *purpose* is what the author or community wanted the text to do: to teach, to warn, to comfort, to record a law or to shape worship. The date matters too. A psalm written for the Temple in Jerusalem reads differently when you know the Temple still stood. A prophecy spoken during a war reads differently when you know the war. Scholars call this setting the text's *context*.

None of this limits what a text means to believers today. Christians read Luke as speaking to them, not only to Theophilus. But a careful reader starts with the first audience and then asks how later communities have read the same words. A historian reading Luke asks the same questions a reader of Paul or the Qur'an would ask.

words.d: the people a text was first written or spoken for
what an author or community wanted a text to do, such as teach, warn or guide worship
the time, place and situation in which a text was written or first heard

look.title: An Author Explains Himself
look.text: It seemed good to me also, having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order, most excellent Theophilus, That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed.
look.cite: Gospel of Luke 1:3-4, King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: Find the audience and the purpose in these two verses. What words tell you each one?

check.q: In Luke 1:3-4, who is named as the reader of the Gospel?
check.why: The author of Luke says he is writing an orderly account for most excellent Theophilus.

check.q: What purpose does the author of Luke give for writing?
choices: To record the laws of the Temple
So the reader may know the certainty of what he was taught
check.why: Luke 1:4 says the author writes so that the reader might know the certainty of the things he was taught.

check.q: A reader learns that a prophecy was spoken during a war. What is the reader paying attention to?
check.why: The time, place and situation of a text are its context, which helps explain what it says.

lessons.title: The Careful Reader's Questions
lessons.mainIdea: Asking who, to whom, when and why turns a hard passage into one you can explain, even when some answers are uncertain.
reading: Try the questions on a text from far away. The Dhammapada is a collection of short verses in the Pali language. Buddhists hold that the verses record teachings of the Buddha, who lived in northern India, probably in the fifth century BCE. Monks memorized and recited them for generations before they were written down. The audience was anyone seeking the path the Buddha taught, especially monks and nuns.

Now read its first verse in Max Müller's 1881 English translation: All that we are is the result of what we have thought. With the questions in mind, you can see what the verse is doing. It is not a history lesson. It is a *teaching*, meant to train the mind. Its purpose is practical: if thoughts shape a person, then guarding one's thoughts is the first step on the path.

Sometimes the answers are uncertain. For many ancient texts, no one knows the exact date or writer. That is fine. A careful reader says what is known, what is traditional and what scholars debate. You might write: Buddhists attribute these verses to the Buddha; scholars date the collection's written form to centuries after his life. That sentence is honest about *evidence*, the facts that support a claim.

Use four questions for every text in this course. Who wrote or gave it, according to the tradition and to scholars? Who was its first audience? When and where did it come from? Why was it made, and why do people still read it? You will not always get full answers, but you will always read more carefully.

words.d: a text or saying meant to instruct listeners in how to think or live
the facts or sources that support a claim
a collection of short verses in Pali that Buddhists hold records teachings of the Buddha

look.title: The First Verse of the Dhammapada
look.text: All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts.
look.cite: Dhammapada, chapter 1, verse 1, translated by F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 10, 1881
look.prompt: Using the four questions, explain what kind of text this is and what it was meant to do for its first hearers.

check.q: Who was the first audience of the Dhammapada, according to the lesson?
choices: People seeking the Buddha's path, especially monks and nuns
check.why: The Dhammapada's verses were recited for those seeking the path the Buddha taught, especially monks and nuns.

check.q: What kind of text is the first verse of the Dhammapada?
choices: A teaching meant to train the mind
check.why: The verse says that thoughts shape a person, so it works as a teaching meant to train the mind.

check.q: What should a careful reader do when the date or writer of a text is uncertain?
choices: Say what is known, what is traditional and what scholars debate
check.why: Honest reading separates what is known, what the tradition holds and what scholars debate, based on the evidence.

lessons.title: Oral Tradition Before Writing
lessons.mainIdea: Many sacred texts were memorized and recited for generations before anyone wrote them down, and recitation still matters today.
reading: In parts of India today, young students still learn the Vedas the old way. A teacher chants a line, and the students repeat it, again and again, with exact rhythm and pitch. They learn to chant each hymn in several patterns, even word by word backward, so that no syllable slips. For well over two thousand years, this method passed down the Vedic hymns mostly by voice. Scholars call this *oral tradition*: knowledge handed down by speaking and memory.

Other traditions began the same way. Buddhist tradition holds that after the Buddha died, his followers met and recited his teachings together to fix them in memory. According to tradition, the Pali Canon was first written down in Sri Lanka in the first century BCE. Jewish tradition speaks of an Oral Torah given alongside the written one. It was passed from teacher to student and later recorded in the Mishnah, around 200 CE.

Memory still matters. Many Muslims memorize the entire Qur'an, more than six thousand verses in Arabic. A person who does so is honored with the title *hafiz*, meaning guardian or one who preserves. During the month of Ramadan, many mosques hold night prayers in which a hafiz recites the whole Qur'an over the month. *Recitation*, reading or chanting aloud from memory, is a central way many traditions keep their texts.

For readers, oral tradition is a reminder that many sacred texts were meant first to be heard. Repetition, rhythm and lists that seem strange on a page often make sense when you imagine them spoken aloud to a crowd. A psalm, a sutra or a surah may have been sung or chanted long before it was ever copied onto a page.

words.d: knowledge, stories or teachings handed down by speaking and memory rather than writing
in Islam, a person who has memorized the whole Qur'an; the word means guardian
reading or chanting a text aloud, often from memory

look.title: Words to Speak Aloud
look.text: And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart: And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
look.prompt: How does this passage expect its words to be passed on? Point to the phrases that describe speaking and repeating.

check.q: What is oral tradition?
choices: Knowledge handed down by speaking and memory
check.why: Oral tradition passes teachings from person to person by speech and memory rather than writing.

check.q: What title is given to a Muslim who has memorized the whole Qur'an?
check.why: A hafiz, meaning guardian, is a person who has memorized the entire Qur'an.

check.q: According to Jewish tradition, what happened to the Oral Torah?
choices: It was passed from teacher to student and later recorded in the Mishnah
check.why: Jewish tradition holds the Oral Torah was passed down by teachers and later recorded in the Mishnah, around 200 CE.

lessons.title: Scrolls, Codices and Palm Leaves
lessons.mainIdea: The form a text is written on, from scroll to codex to palm leaf to printed book, shapes how people read and use it.
reading: In 1947, shepherds near the Dead Sea found clay jars in a cave, holding ancient scrolls. More finds followed in nearby caves near a site called Qumran. The Dead Sea Scrolls include the oldest known copies of books of the Hebrew Bible, some dating to the third or second century BCE. They are written on parchment, specially prepared animal skin, and on papyrus. They are *scrolls*: long sheets rolled up and read by unrolling.

Early Christians favored a different form, the *codex*, the ancestor of the modern book. A codex is made of sheets folded and sewn along one edge. It can hold more text than one scroll and lets a reader flip quickly between passages. Scholars note that surviving early Christian writings are mostly codices, while Jewish communities kept the scroll for the Torah read in worship, a custom that continues today.

In South and Southeast Asia, many texts were written on *palm-leaf manuscripts*. Scribes cut and dried the leaves of certain palms, scratched letters into them with a metal stylus and rubbed in soot or ink. The leaves were stacked and tied with cord through holes, like the one in the museum story. Because leaves decay in a humid climate, texts had to be copied again and again. Many Buddhist and Hindu texts survive this way.

Printing changed things again. Johannes Gutenberg's Bible, printed in Mainz around 1455, helped make identical copies common in Europe. Yet many communities still honor handwritten copies. A kosher Torah scroll must be written by hand by a trained scribe, and Qur'an calligraphy remains a treasured art.

words.d: long sheets of parchment or papyrus that are rolled up and read by unrolling
an early form of the book, made of sheets folded and sewn along one edge
texts written by hand on dried palm leaves, common in South and Southeast Asia
ancient Jewish scrolls found near Qumran beginning in 1947, including the oldest known copies of Hebrew Bible books

look.title: Finding a Verse
look.text: Two readers want to compare a line near the beginning of a long book with a line near the end. One has the text on a single scroll twenty feet long. The other has it as a codex with numbered pages.
look.prompt: Describe what each reader has to do. Why might a community that often compared passages come to prefer the codex?

check.q: Where were the Dead Sea Scrolls found, beginning in 1947?
choices: In a temple in Sri Lanka
In caves near Qumran by the Dead Sea
check.why: The Dead Sea Scrolls were found in caves near Qumran, beginning with a shepherd's find in 1947.

check.q: What is a codex?
choices: A scroll wound on two handles
Sheets folded and sewn along one edge, like a book
check.why: A codex is the ancestor of the modern book, made of sheets folded and sewn along one edge.

check.q: Why did palm-leaf texts have to be copied again and again?
choices: Palm leaves decay in a humid climate
check.why: Palm leaves decay in humid climates, so scribes recopied texts to keep them alive.

lessons.title: Canon: Deciding What Is In
lessons.mainIdea: A canon is a community's list of authoritative books, and different communities have drawn the list in different ways.
reading: Pick up a Catholic Bible and a Protestant Bible and count the books. The Catholic Old Testament has 46 books. The Protestant one has 39. The difference comes from books such as Tobit, Judith and 1 and 2 Maccabees. Catholics and Orthodox Christians count them as scripture. Protestants call them the Apocrypha and usually leave them out or print them separately. The word *canon* names a community's official list of sacred books.

Canon comes from a Greek word for a measuring rod. A canon measures which books count. Canons usually form slowly, as communities keep reading certain books in worship and stop reading others. For the Christian New Testament, an important moment came in 367 CE. That year Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, sent a letter listing the 27 books that make up the New Testament today.

The Jewish Tanakh contains the same writings as the Protestant Old Testament but counts and orders them differently, as 24 books. Other traditions draw their boundaries in other ways. The Pali Canon of Theravada Buddhism is huge, and Mahayana Buddhists add many other sutras. Hinduism has no single closed canon at all. Instead, Hindus speak of shruti, what was heard, and *smriti*, what was remembered, a wider group including the epics.

When you compare traditions, ask what counts as scripture for this community, and who decided. The answer is often different from what an outsider expects. A Catholic, a Protestant and a Jewish reader may each hold a book called the Bible and still hold different lists. Asking about the canon helps you know which texts are being compared.

words.d: a community's official list of books it accepts as scripture; from a Greek word for measuring rod
books such as Tobit and Judith that Catholics and Orthodox include in the Old Testament and Protestants usually do not
in Hinduism, what was remembered: honored texts such as the epics, distinct from the Vedas

look.title: Counting the Books
look.cite: Standard traditional counts; the Tanakh and the Protestant Old Testament contain the same writings, divided differently
look.prompt: The Tanakh and the Protestant Old Testament have the same content but different counts. What does that tell you about comparing numbers without context?

check.q: What does the word canon originally mean?
check.why: Canon comes from a Greek word for measuring rod; a canon measures which books count as scripture.

check.q: Why does a Catholic Old Testament have more books than a Protestant one?
choices: Catholics split every book into two
Catholics add the Gospels to the Old Testament
Catholics include books such as Tobit and Judith
check.why: Catholics and Orthodox include books such as Tobit, Judith and Maccabees, which Protestants call the Apocrypha.

check.q: What did Athanasius do in 367 CE?
choices: Listed the 27 books of today's New Testament in a letter
check.why: In 367 CE, Athanasius of Alexandria listed the 27 books that make up the New Testament today.

sections.title: Kinds of Texts, Ways of Studying

lessons.title: Law, Story and Poetry
lessons.mainIdea: Sacred texts contain many genres, and each genre asks to be read in its own way.
reading: Read three passages from the Hebrew Bible side by side. Exodus 20 gives commands: honor your father and mother, do not steal. Genesis 12 tells a story: God calls Abram to leave his country, and he goes. Psalm 23 sings: The LORD is my shepherd. All three are sacred to Jews and Christians, but they work differently. Scholars call these kinds of writing *genre*, a type of text with its own form and purpose.

*Law* tells people what to do or not do. It is often short, direct and specific, and it may include cases: if this happens, then do that. Readers of law ask who it applies to and how it has been interpreted. *Narrative*, or story, has characters, events and a plot. Readers of narrative ask what happens, why, and what the story shows about God, people or the world.

*Poetry* uses images, rhythm and repetition. Hebrew poetry often uses parallelism, saying one idea twice in slightly different words. A shepherd in a psalm is an image, not a job description. Readers of poetry ask what feelings and pictures the words create. Reading a poem as if it were a law, or a law as if it were a poem, leads to confusion.

Other traditions have their own genres. The Qur'an contains stories of earlier prophets, legal guidance and passages of intense rhythmic beauty. The Hindu epics are vast narratives. Knowing the genre of a passage is one of the first steps in reading it well.

words.d: a kind of writing, such as law, story or poetry, with its own form and purpose
a genre that gives commands, rules or cases telling people what to do
a genre that tells a story, with characters, events and a plot
a genre that uses images, rhythm and repetition; Hebrew poetry often uses parallelism

look.title: A Shepherd in a Poem
look.text: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters.
look.prompt: What genre is this passage? What picture does the image of a shepherd create, and why does it matter to read it as poetry?

check.q: Genesis 12, where God calls Abram to leave his country, is an example of which genre?
check.why: Genesis 12 tells a story with a character and events, so it is narrative.

check.q: What is parallelism in Hebrew poetry?
choices: Printing two translations side by side
Saying one idea twice in slightly different words
check.why: Hebrew poetry often uses parallelism, repeating one idea in slightly different words.

check.q: Why does it matter to know that Psalm 23 is poetry?
choices: Poetry is always less important than law
The shepherd is an image to interpret, not a job description
Poetry was never used in worship
check.why: Reading Psalm 23 as poetry means reading the shepherd as an image that creates a picture of care.

lessons.title: Prophecy, Letter and Teaching
lessons.mainIdea: Prophecy speaks a message to a people, letters answer a community's questions and teachings instruct, and each shapes how a passage reads.
reading: In the eighth century BCE, a herdsman named Amos went to the northern kingdom of Israel with a hard message. According to the book that bears his name, he condemned people who held religious festivals while cheating the poor. This is *prophecy*: a message that the prophet presents as coming from God, often a warning or call to change. In the Hebrew Bible, prophecy is less about predicting the future than about speaking to the present.

Some sacred texts are *letters*, written to real people about real problems. Paul's first letter to the Corinthians answers questions the church in Corinth had sent him, about food, marriage and worship. A reader who knows it is a letter looks for the problem behind each answer. One side of a conversation is on the page, and the other side has to be pieced together.

Other texts are *teachings*: sayings, dialogues and instructions from a teacher. The Analects record short sayings of Confucius and conversations with his students. The Bhagavad Gita is a dialogue in which Krishna teaches the warrior Arjuna. The Dhammapada gathers verses Buddhists attribute to the Buddha. Teachings are often brief, quotable and meant to be memorized and practiced.

Many books mix genres. The Gospels contain narrative, teaching, parables and prophecy. The Qur'an moves among warning, law, story and praise. Naming the genre of each passage, not just each book, keeps you from misreading it. A single chapter can shift from one genre to another in a few verses.

words.d: a message a prophet presents as coming from God, often a warning or a call to change
texts written to real people or communities, such as Paul's letters to early churches
sayings, dialogues or instructions from a teacher, meant to be learned and practiced

look.title: A Prophet's Demand
look.text: But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.
look.cite: Amos 5:24, King James Version (1611); judgment here means justice
look.prompt: This verse follows a passage criticizing festivals held while the poor were cheated. What is the prophet asking for, and how does knowing the genre help you read it?

check.q: According to the lesson, what is prophecy in the Hebrew Bible mostly about?
choices: Predicting dates far in the future
Speaking a message to the present, often a warning or call to change
check.why: Hebrew Bible prophecy, like that of Amos, is mostly a message to its own time presented as coming from God.

check.q: Why does a reader of 1 Corinthians look for the problem behind each answer?
choices: Because it is a letter responding to the church's questions
Because it is a law code
Because it was written on palm leaves
check.why: First Corinthians is a letter answering questions the church in Corinth had sent Paul, so only one side of the conversation is on the page.

check.q: Which text is a dialogue in which a teacher instructs a student?
choices: The Bhagavad Gita, where Krishna teaches Arjuna
check.why: The Bhagavad Gita is a dialogue in which Krishna teaches the warrior Arjuna, a teaching text.

lessons.title: Studying Religion in a Public School
lessons.mainIdea: Public schools may teach about religion objectively, which is different from practicing or promoting a faith.
reading: In 1963, the U.S. Supreme Court decided a case called Abington School District v. Schempp. A Pennsylvania family objected to a law requiring daily Bible readings as religious exercises in public schools. The Court ruled that such devotional readings violated the *First Amendment*, which forbids government from establishing religion. But the Court also said that studying the Bible or religion objectively, as part of a secular education, is permitted.

That ruling draws the line this course follows. *Devotional* reading is reading a text in order to worship, pray or grow in faith. It belongs to families and religious communities. The *academic study of religion* reads the same texts to understand them: their history, their meaning to adherents, and their influence on the world. A student of any faith, or of no faith, can do this work.

Academic study has a few habits. It describes rather than judges. It attributes every belief: Hindus believe, according to the Qur'an. It uses each tradition's own terms and explains them. It shows the variety inside each tradition. And it stays *neutral*, neither promoting nor attacking any religion. The goal is understanding, not agreement.

This course lives by those habits. You will be asked what a text says, what a community believes about it and how two traditions answer the same question. You will not be asked to believe or reject any of it. Your own beliefs are your own, and they are welcome in your life outside the assignment.

words.d: the part of the U.S. Constitution that protects free exercise of religion and forbids government from establishing one
done in order to worship, pray or grow in faith
the study of religions to understand their texts, beliefs, practices and history, without promoting or rejecting them
not taking a side; in this course, neither promoting nor attacking any religion

look.title: What the Court Allowed
look.text: The Court did not say the Bible must be kept out of schools. It said that study of the Bible or of religion, when it is presented objectively as part of a secular program of education, is consistent with the First Amendment.
look.cite: Abington School District v. Schempp, U.S. Supreme Court, 1963, majority opinion by Justice Tom C. Clark (paraphrased)
look.prompt: What is the difference between the Bible readings the Court struck down and the kind of study it allowed?

check.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in Abington School District v. Schempp (1963)?
choices: Religion may never be mentioned in school
Devotional Bible readings in public schools were unconstitutional, but objective study is allowed
Only private schools may own Bibles
check.why: The Court struck down required devotional readings but said objective study of religion in a secular education is permitted.

check.q: Which activity is devotional rather than academic?
choices: Comparing how two traditions read one verse
Explaining what Muslims believe about the Qur'an
Reading a psalm in order to pray
check.why: Reading a text in order to pray is devotional; the other activities aim at understanding, which is academic.

check.q: Which sentence follows the habits of the academic study of religion?
choices: According to the Qur'an, God is one.
Our religion is better than theirs.
check.why: The first sentence attributes the belief to its source and stays neutral, which is how academic study describes religion.

review.q: Which statement best describes what makes a text sacred, as scholars use the term?
choices: A community sets it apart and lives by it
Its use of an ancient language
review.why: A sacred text is defined by its relationship to a community that treats it as holy or authoritative.

review.q: Which pair matches a tradition with the belief about its text's origin?
choices: Buddhists: the Qur'an was heard by sages
Sikhs: the Vedas were written by Moses
Muslims: the Qur'an was revealed to Muhammad
Hindus: the Torah was given at Sinai
review.why: Muslims believe the Qur'an was revealed by God to Muhammad; the other pairs mix up traditions and texts.

review.q: The four questions of a careful reader are who, to whom, when and what else?
review.why: A careful reader asks who made a text, for whom, when, and why, that is, its purpose.

review.q: What do the Vedic chanting of India and the hafiz tradition in Islam have in common?
choices: Both preserve sacred texts through memory and recitation
review.why: Both traditions keep sacred texts through oral memorization and recitation.

review.q: Why do Jewish communities still use a handwritten scroll for the Torah read in worship?
choices: A kosher Torah scroll must be written by hand by a trained scribe
Printing is forbidden in all religions
The Dead Sea Scrolls require it
review.why: Jewish practice requires a Torah scroll for worship to be handwritten by a trained scribe, keeping the scroll form alive.

review.q: The Tanakh has 24 books and the Protestant Old Testament has 39. Why?
choices: They contain the same writings counted and ordered differently
review.why: The Tanakh and the Protestant Old Testament contain the same writings but divide and count them differently.

review.q: A reader notices that a passage speaks to real people about a problem they had written about. Which genre is it most likely?
review.why: Letters, such as Paul's letters to the Corinthians, answer real people's questions and problems.

review.q: What is the main goal of the academic study of religion in a public school?
choices: Understanding religions without promoting or rejecting them
review.why: Academic study aims at understanding and stays neutral, as the Supreme Court described in the Schempp case.
